To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
social decision-making recruits many of the same brain areas that are involved in non-social decisions.

(i) social decision-making recruits a network of brain areas involved in reward and punishment, mentalization, and emotion regulation; and (ii) the prefrontal and temporal cortices are important for prudent social decision-making.

social decision-making engages a distributed network of brain regions that includes the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and insula, as well as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain supports the complex and dynamic decisions that we make in our social environments.
understanding how social decisions are implemented in the human brain, with the ultimate goal of informing the design of social decision-making interventions.
understanding the neural systems that support social cognition, and with the neural bases of social decision-making.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
social decision-making is a complex phenomenon that engages many brain regions and systems, and that there is much more to be done to better understand this important aspect of our social lives.
the neural systems that support social decision-making are complex, and are still under active investigation.

social decisions are supported by a distributed neural system, and that this system is highly flexible in its recruitment and function.
The neuroscience of social decisions
Bartolo, Raff
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the neural systems that support social decision-making are complex, but also highly flexible, with a variety of neural systems being recruited depending on the context of the social decision and the individual making the decision.

we are just beginning to understand the neural systems that support social decisions, and that this knowledge has important implications for understanding social behavior in general, and social psychopathology in particular.
the social brain is not just a brain for social cognition, but a brain for social action.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social decision-making is a complex process involving many brain regions and systems that work together to support the decisions we make in social environments.
the human brain is highly flexible and can be adapted to a wide range of social environments, but that it is also constrained by the social environments that it evolved in.

social decision-making is a highly complex and multifaceted process that involves multiple brain systems, and that the brain’s ability to flexibly integrate information from these different systems is crucial to prudent social decision-making in complex and changing environments.
